newsitem.title: USA: Gitano founder, three others settle insider suit.
newsitem.headline: Gitano founder, three others settle insider suit.

text.p: The founder of Gitano Group Inc and three former executives agreed to pay $1.1 million in penalties to settle insider trading charges, federal regulators said Wednesday.
The Securities and Exchange Commission said the group settled a civil complaint filed in a Manhattan federal court without admitting or denying wrongdoing.

The SEC alleged that the founder, Morris Dabah, who was also former chief executive of the company, and former executive vice president Robert Reiss traded Gitano stock in early 1992 using company financial information.
Dabah allegedly sold shares in March 1992 through a Luxembourg bank, days before Gitano announced it had lost $71 million for 1991.
Reiss allegedly bought shares through an account at a Swiss bank on May 3, 1992, the day before Gitano announced favorable first quarter 1992 earnings of $6 million.

And on June 16 of the same year, Dabah, Reiss and Stanley Greenstein, the former chief financial officer, all sold shares before the company disclosed that a lender to its Hong Kong subsidiary had imposed a security condition on a credit facility, the SEC said.
The SEC alleged all three knew the lender had threatened to terminate the credit line when they sold.

The fourth defendant, David Keery, former finance officer who reported to Greenstein, allegedly failed to promptly put up a reserve for losses Gitano suffered in a deal with Skiva International. That resulted in the deferred reporting of $3.3 million in losses, the SEC said.
The SEC said that in the settlement, Dabah agreed to pay $266,237 and Greenstein $236,982, representing losses illegally avoided when they sold Gitano stock, plus prejudgment interest.
Reiss agreed to pay $79,831, the amount of his alleged illegal profits and losses avoided.
Dabah, Reiss, Greenstein and Keery agreed to pay civil penalties of $186,877, $79,825, $167,437 and $25,000, respectively.
Gitano, which was based in Manhattan at the time of the alleged wrongdoing, was purchased for $100 million by Fruit of the Loom Inc in 1994.
